text:
My own list isn’t especially flattering: I’m impulsive, and I idealize too much, although I don’t demonize. I’m very open and not very private. I care more about honesty than the standard romantic ideal. I still love my exes. After being deeply in love, I have overly high expectations, so I’m hard to please with a basic relationship.

I’m also extremely unique and have deeply held convictions many people won’t agree with. I’m anti-vax, anti-money, anti-civilization, etc. And I’m not yet living the way I want to live (astrology predicts I will by 2030 😃).

A woman should know that before she starts fitting me into the life or fantasy she already planned.

Key was an inner-child therapist and Reiki healer. Both Key and Bee were extremely curious and open-minded, which I loved about them. They were open to spiritual experiences, very connected to childlike wonder, and were always seeing what they needed to work on. They both meditated a lot.

I saw all that and thought anyone with that much spiritual depth and curiosity must already be far along on the path.

That was my mistake. Their meditations may have helped them a lot. I still had no idea how either woman would act when a relationship got ugly. If somebody starts with enough trauma, huge progress can still leave a lot unresolved.

My own blind spot is that I have trouble understanding where people are at mentally and emotionally. A partner may agree with everything I say and then tell me later, “Didn’t you understand I was FAWNING?”

No, I really didn’t. If you’re fawning, tell me when you can, because I can’t know what’s happening in your head just because it feels obvious to you.
reader: Someone getting to know a new partner, deciding what to tell them about their own flaws and what to ask.

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
